title: Y and en
topic: the pronouns y and en; pronouns in the passé composé and participle agreement
why: This lesson introduces y and en, two very frequent pronouns with no English equivalent, for places, things and quantities. It also shows where pronouns go in the passé composé and when the participle agrees with a direct object placed before it.

{"lessons": ["

Y: there, about it

English has nothing quite like y and en, two tiny words that French uses all the time to avoid repeating a place or a thing. Let's start with y.

Y replaces a place

After à, en, chez, dans, sur…, y means \"there\". It goes before the verb, like the other pronouns.

Tu vas à Lyon ? — Oui, j'y vais demain.Are you going to Lyon? — Yes, I'm going (there) tomorrow.
Elle habite en Bretagne ? — Oui, elle y habite depuis dix ans.Does she live in Brittany? — Yes, she's lived there for ten years.
Tu vas chez le médecin ? — Non, je n'y vais pas.Are you going to the doctor's? — No, I'm not (going).

English often just drops \"there\" (\"Yes, I'm going\"), but French can't: Je vais alone is incomplete. Say J'y vais.

Y replaces à + a thing

With verbs built with à, like penser à or répondre à, y replaces a thing or an idea: \"about it\", \"to it\".

Tu penses à ton examen ? — Oui, j'y pense souvent.Are you thinking about your exam? — Yes, I often think about it.
à + thingà + person
Je réponds à la lettre. → J'y réponds.Je réponds à Paul. → Je lui réponds.

With an infinitive, y goes before it: Je vais y aller. And you'll hear one phrase every day: On y va ! (Let's go!).

Remember the fixed form Vas-y ! (Go on!): the -s comes back so you can pronounce the liaison, « va-z-y ».

", "

En: some, of it, of them

En replaces a noun introduced by de: a partitive (du, de la, des), a quantity, or a verb built with de.

Partitives: some, any

Tu veux du café ? — Oui, j'en veux bien. / Non merci, je n'en veux pas.Do you want some coffee? — Yes, I'd love some. / No thanks, I don't want any.

English says \"some\" or \"any\", or nothing at all (\"Yes, please\"). French needs en.

Quantities and numbers

With a number or a quantity, en replaces the noun, and the number or the quantity stays at the end:

QuestionAnswer with en
Tu as des enfants ?Oui, j'en ai deux.
Il y a des pommes ?Oui, il y en a beaucoup.
Vous voulez combien de tomates ?J'en voudrais un kilo.
Tu bois du lait ?Non, je n'en bois jamais.

Never J'ai deux alone: J'en ai deux (I have two of them). And il y a becomes il y en a (there is some, there are some).

Verbs with de

Tu parles de ton voyage ? — Oui, j'en parle à mes amis !Are you talking about your trip? — Yes, I talk about it with my friends!
Tu as besoin de la voiture ? — Non, je n'en ai pas besoin.Do you need the car? — No, I don't need it.

En also replaces a place after venir de: Tu viens de la boulangerie ? — Oui, j'en viens.

A very useful phrase: Je m'en occupe = I'll take care of it (from s'occuper de).

", "

Pronouns in the passé composé

In the passé composé, every pronoun goes before the auxiliary, never before the participle:

PronounAffirmativeNegative
le, la, lesJe l'ai vu.Je ne l'ai pas vu.
lui, leurJe lui ai parlé.Je ne lui ai pas parlé.
yJ'y suis allé.Je n'y suis pas allé.
enJ'en ai mangé.Je n'en ai pas mangé.

The participle agrees with a direct object placed before it

Until now, the participle with avoir never changed. New rule: when a direct object pronoun (le, la, les, me, te, nous, vous) comes before avoir, the participle agrees with it, like an adjective.

Les clés ? Je les ai trouvées.The keys? I found them. (les = les clés, feminine plural)
La lettre ? Je l'ai écrite hier.The letter? I wrote it yesterday.
Léa ? Je l'ai vue au marché.Léa? I saw her at the market.

Most of the time you can't hear it (trouvé, trouvées sound the same), but you can with participles ending in a consonant: écrit / écrite, pris / prise, mis / mise, fait / faite.

No agreement with en or with lui / leur, which are not direct objects: Des pommes ? J'en ai acheté. / Ma sœur ? Je lui ai téléphoné.

Before writing the participle, ask: is there le, la, les (or me, te…) before avoir? If yes, find what it stands for and agree.
